questions.q: Find the mean and median of the data set: $4, 7, 7, 9, 13$.
questions.answer: Mean $=\frac{4+7+7+9+13}{5}=\frac{40}{5}=8$. Median (middle value of the ordered list): $7$.
questions.explanation: Mean $=\frac{4+7+7+9+13}{5}=\frac{40}{5}=8$. Median (middle value of the ordered list): $7$.

questions.q: A sixth data point of $40$ is added to the set $4,7,7,9,13$. Recompute the mean and median, and explain which measure changed more.
questions.answer: New mean $=\frac{40+40}{6}=\frac{80}{6}\approx13.33$. New median (ordered $4,7,7,9,13,40$, average of the two middle values $7$ and $9$): $8$. The mean changed drastically (from $8$ to $13.33$) while the median barely moved (from $7$ to $8$), since the mean is sensitive to the extreme outlier $40$ while the median is resistant to it.
questions.explanation: New mean $=\frac{40+40}{6}=\frac{80}{6}\approx13.33$. New median (ordered $4,7,7,9,13,40$, average of the two middle values $7$ and $9$): $8$. The mean changed drastically (from $8$ to $13.33$) while the median barely moved (from $7$ to $8$), since the mean is sensitive to the extreme outlier $40$ while the median is resistant to it.

questions.q: Find the five-number summary (min, $Q_1$, median, $Q_3$, max) of the ordered data: $2,5,6,9,11,14,15,18,20$.
Using the five-number summary from the previous problem, find the IQR and determine whether $20$ would be flagged as an outlier using the $1.5\times$IQR rule.
questions.answer: IQR $=Q_3-Q_1=16.5-5.5=11$. Upper fence $=Q_3+1.5(11)=16.5+16.5=33$ (using the $1.5\times$IQR rule). Since $20<33$, it is not flagged as an outlier.
questions.explanation: IQR $=Q_3-Q_1=16.5-5.5=11$. Upper fence $=Q_3+1.5(11)=16.5+16.5=33$ (using the $1.5\times$IQR rule). Since $20<33$, it is not flagged as an outlier.

questions.q: Find the standard deviation of the data set $2,4,6,8$ (treat as a population).
questions.answer: Mean $=5$. Deviations: $-3,-1,1,3$. Squared deviations: $9,1,1,9$, sum $=20$. Variance $=\frac{20}{4}=5$. Standard deviation $=\sqrt{5}\approx2.24$.
questions.explanation: Mean $=5$. Deviations: $-3,-1,1,3$. Squared deviations: $9,1,1,9$, sum $=20$. Variance $=\frac{20}{4}=5$. Standard deviation $=\sqrt{5}\approx2.24$.

questions.q: Explain why the standard deviation is always non-negative, and why it equals $0$ only in one specific case.
questions.answer: The standard deviation is the square root of an average of squared deviations, and squares are always non-negative, so their average and its square root are also non-negative. It equals $0$ only when every data value is identical (no spread at all), since that is the only case where every deviation from the mean is $0$.
questions.explanation: The standard deviation is the square root of an average of squared deviations, and squares are always non-negative, so their average and its square root are also non-negative. It equals $0$ only when every data value is identical (no spread at all), since that is the only case where every deviation from the mean is $0$.

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: Class A has a mean test score of $80$ with a standard deviation of $4$. Class B has a mean of $80$ with a standard deviation of $12$. Compare the two classes' consistency, and explain what a small vs. large standard deviation indicates.
questions.target: Comparing distributions using measures of spread
questions.answer: Both classes have the same average performance (mean $80$), but Class A's scores are tightly clustered around the mean (small spread, standard deviation $4$), meaning most students scored similarly, while Class B's scores are much more spread out (standard deviation $12$), meaning there is far more variability — some students scored well above or below the average.
questions.explanation: Both classes have the same average performance (mean $80$), but Class A's scores are tightly clustered around the mean (small spread, standard deviation $4$), meaning most students scored similarly, while Class B's scores are much more spread out (standard deviation $12$), meaning there is far more variability — some students scored well above or below the average.

questions.q: Explain why the median and IQR are described as "resistant" measures, while the mean and standard deviation are not, using the outlier example from earlier in this worksheet as a reference.
questions.answer: A resistant measure is one that is not strongly affected by extreme values or outliers. The median and IQR depend only on the position (ranking) of data values, not their exact size, so a single extreme value has little effect on them. The mean and standard deviation, in contrast, use every data value's actual size in their calculation, so one extreme outlier (like the $40$ added earlier) can shift them substantially.

The median and IQR depend only on the position (ranking) of data values, not their exact size, so a single extreme value has little effect on them. The mean and standard deviation, in contrast, use every data value's actual size in their calculation, so one extreme outlier (like the $40$ added earlier) can shift them substantially.

questions.q: A data set of home prices in a neighborhood is strongly skewed right due to a few very expensive mansions. Recommend which pair of summary statistics (mean/standard deviation or median/IQR) should be reported, and justify your choice.
questions.answer: The median and IQR should be reported, since they are resistant to the effect of the few extremely expensive mansions. Reporting the mean would give a misleadingly high sense of a "typical" home price, since the mean is pulled upward by the small number of very high values.
questions.explanation: The median and IQR should be reported, since they are resistant to the effect of the few extremely expensive mansions. Reporting the mean would give a misleadingly high sense of a "typical" home price, since the mean is pulled upward by the small number of very high values.

questions.q: A quality-control process measures the diameter of manufactured bolts, which are expected to be very consistent (low variability) and roughly symmetric. Recommend which pair of summary statistics is more appropriate here, and explain why.
questions.answer: The mean and standard deviation are appropriate here, since the data is roughly symmetric with no extreme outliers expected — in this case, the mean and standard deviation use all the data efficiently and are the standard choice when a distribution is not skewed.
questions.explanation: The mean and standard deviation are appropriate here, since the data is roughly symmetric with no extreme outliers expected — in this case, the mean and standard deviation use all the data efficiently and are the standard choice when a distribution is not skewed.

questions.q: A survey of families records number of children per household: 0 children (8 families), 1 child (15 families), 2 children (20 families), 3 children (7 families). Find the mean number of children per household.
questions.target: Computing summary statistics from a frequency table
questions.answer: Total families: $8+15+20+7=50$. Total children: $0(8)+1(15)+2(20)+3(7)=0+15+40+21=76$. Mean $=\frac{76}{50}=1.52$ children per household.
questions.explanation: Total families: $8+15+20+7=50$. Total children: $0(8)+1(15)+2(20)+3(7)=0+15+40+21=76$. Mean $=\frac{76}{50}=1.52$ children per household.

questions.q: A small business records weekly sales (in thousands): $10, 12, 12, 14, 17$. Find the mean, and then find the variance and standard deviation (treat as a population).
questions.target: Computing summary statistics from a frequency table
questions.answer: Mean $=\frac{10+12+12+14+17}{5}=\frac{65}{5}=13$. Deviations: $-3,-1,-1,1,4$. Squared: $9,1,1,1,16$, sum $=28$. Variance $=\frac{28}{5}=5.6$. Standard deviation $=\sqrt{5.6}\approx2.37$.
questions.explanation: Mean $=\frac{10+12+12+14+17}{5}=\frac{65}{5}=13$. Deviations: $-3,-1,-1,1,4$. Squared: $9,1,1,1,16$, sum $=28$. Variance $=\frac{28}{5}=5.6$. Standard deviation $=\sqrt{5.6}\approx2.37$.

questions.q: Two data sets both represent quiz scores out of 20 for two different classes of the same size, and both have the same mean of 15. Class A has a standard deviation of 1.2, while Class B has a standard deviation of 4.5. Without doing any further calculation, describe what a dotplot of each class's scores would likely look like, and explain how you can tell just from the two standard deviations.
questions.target: Computing summary statistics from a frequency table
questions.answer: Class A's dotplot would show scores tightly clustered close to 15 (most students scoring similarly, in a narrow band), since a small standard deviation of 1.2 indicates little spread around the mean. Class B's dotplot would show scores much more spread out around 15, with a substantial number of students scoring noticeably above or below the mean, since a standard deviation of 4.5 indicates far greater variability.
questions.explanation: Class A's dotplot would show scores tightly clustered close to 15 (most students scoring similarly, in a narrow band), since a small standard deviation of 1.2 indicates little spread around the mean. Class B's dotplot would show scores much more spread out around 15, with a substantial number of students scoring noticeably above or below the mean, since a standard deviation of 4.5 indicates far greater variability.

sections.heading: Part III — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (15–20)

questions.q: A coach records the vertical jump heights (in inches) of 7 athletes: $22, 24, 25, 26, 26, 28, 41$. Explain why the value $41$ would likely be flagged as an outlier, and describe, in general terms, the two-step process for using the $1.5\times$IQR rule to formally check whether a value is an outlier.
questions.target: Computing summary statistics from a frequency table
questions.answer: The value $41$ is far larger than the rest of the data (which clusters between 22 and 28), so it looks like a clear outlier by visual inspection. Formally, the $1.5\times$IQR rule works in two steps: first compute the IQR ($Q_3-Q_1$) from the five-number summary, then compute the lower fence ($Q_1-1.5\times$IQR) and upper fence ($Q_3+1.5\times$IQR); any value falling below the lower fence or above the upper fence is classified as an outlier.
questions.explanation: The value $41$ is far larger than the rest of the data (which clusters between 22 and 28), so it looks like a clear outlier by visual inspection. Formally, the $1.5\times$IQR rule works in two steps: first compute the IQR ($Q_3-Q_1$) from the five-number summary, then compute the lower fence ($Q_1-1.5\times$IQR) and upper fence ($Q_3+1.5\times$IQR); any value falling below the lower fence or above the upper fence is classified as an outlier.

questions.q: A teacher records the number of minutes 8 students spent on homework last night: $30, 45, 50, 55, 60, 60, 65, 200$. The value $200$ comes from a student who mistakenly reported total weekly homework time instead of just last night. Explain, step by step, how this single incorrect data entry would affect the reported mean versus the reported median, and explain which measure a teacher should trust more when summarizing typical homework time for this data set, given the known data-entry error.
questions.target: Computing summary statistics from a frequency table
questions.answer: The mean would be pulled dramatically upward by the erroneous $200$ value, since the mean uses every data point's exact size — it would suggest students spend far more time on homework than they actually do. The median, which only depends on the middle-ranked value(s), would be far less affected by this single extreme (and erroneous) value. Given the known data-entry error, the teacher should trust the median as a more accurate reflection of typical homework time, since it resists distortion from this kind of outlier.
questions.explanation: The mean would be pulled dramatically upward by the erroneous $200$ value, since the mean uses every data point's exact size — it would suggest students spend far more time on homework than they actually do. The median, which only depends on the middle-ranked value(s), would be far less affected by this single extreme (and erroneous) value. Given the known data-entry error, the teacher should trust the median as a more accurate reflection of typical homework time, since it resists distortion from this kind of outlier.

questions.q: A machine dispenses a liquid into containers. The amount of liquid dispensed, in milliliters, follows a continuous uniform distribution over the interval $[95, 105]$. A quality control inspector randomly selects 5 containers and measures the amount of liquid in each. Let $X_i$ be the amount of liquid in the $i^{th}$ container, for $i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$. The company has implemented a new calibration process that, on average, increases the mean amount of liquid dispensed by $\delta$ milliliters, but also increases the variance by $\sigma^2$. The inspector is specifically looking for evidence that the calibration process has *decreased* the variability of the dispensed liquid while maintaining a satisfactory average fill. If the current calibration process yields a mean fill of $\mu_0 = 100$ ml and a standard deviation of $\sigma_0 = 2$ ml, and the new process is hypothesized to have a mean fill of $\mu_1 = 100 + \delta$ ml and a standard deviation of $\sigma_1 = 2 - \sigma_{dev}$ ml, where $\delta > 0$ and $\sigma_{dev} > 0$ are unknown positive constants, what is the minimum value of $\sigma_{dev}$ such that the probability of falsely concluding that the new process has *increased* variability (i.e., Type I error) is at most $0.01$, assuming the mean fill remains at $100$ ml (i.e., $\delta = 0$)?
questions.target: Comparing distributions using measures of spread
questions.answer: Let $X$ be the amount of liquid dispensed by the machine. $X$ follows a continuous uniform distribution $U(95, 105)$. The mean is $\mu = \frac{95+105}{2} = 100$ ml. The variance is $\sigma^2 = \frac{(105-95)^2}{12} = \frac{100}{12} = \frac{25}{3}$. The standard deviation is $\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{25}{3}} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 2.887$ ml. The problem statement implies the initial standard deviation is $\sigma_0 = 2$ ml, which contradicts the calculated standard deviation for a uniform distribution from 95 to 105. This suggests a misunderstanding in the problem phrasing or that the uniform distribution is a simplified model, and the actual process has a standard deviation of $\sigma_0=2$. We will proceed assuming the standard deviation of the current process is $\sigma_0 = 2$ ml. Final Answer: Approximately $1.37$

The variance is $\sigma^2 = \frac{(105-95)^2}{12} = \frac{100}{12} = \frac{25}{3}$. The standard deviation is $\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{25}{3}} = \frac{5}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 2.887$ ml. We will proceed assuming the standard deviation of the current process is $\sigma_0 = 2$ ml. Final Answer: Approximately $1.37$

questions.q: A set of daily high temperatures in Celsius has mean $\bar{x} = 25.0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and standard deviation $s = 4.0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Convert the temperatures to Fahrenheit using $F = 1.8C + 32$. Find the new mean and standard deviation in Fahrenheit.
questions.answer: Mean: Affected by both multiplication and addition: $\bar{x}_F = 1.8(25.0) + 32 = 45.0 + 32 = \mathbf{77.0^{\circ}\mathrm{F}}.$ Standard Deviation: Affected ONLY by multiplication, not by the addition of 32: $s_F = 1.8(s_C) = 1.8(4.0) = \mathbf{7.2^{\circ}\mathrm{F}}.$
questions.explanation: Mean: Affected by both multiplication and addition: $\bar{x}_F = 1.8(25.0) + 32 = 45.0 + 32 = \mathbf{77.0^{\circ}\mathrm{F}}.$ Standard Deviation: Affected ONLY by multiplication, not by the addition of 32: $s_F = 1.8(s_C) = 1.8(4.0) = \mathbf{7.2^{\circ}\mathrm{F}}.$

questions.q: A pharmaceutical company is conducting a clinical trial to test the efficacy of a new drug designed to lower blood pressure. They recruit 200 participants and randomly assign them to either the treatment group (receiving the new drug) or the control group (receiving a placebo). After 12 weeks, they measure the reduction in systolic blood pressure for each participant. The company wants to perform a hypothesis test to determine if there is a significant difference in blood pressure reduction between the two groups. The trial is designed with 20 participants in the treatment group and 180 participants in the control group. If the standard deviation of blood pressure reduction in the treatment group is $\sigma_1 = 15 \mathrm{\ mmHg}$ and in the control group is $\sigma_2 = 12 \mathrm{\ mmHg}$, and they are planning to use a two-sample t-test, what is the calculated pooled standard deviation $s_p$ if equal variances are assumed, given the following summary statistics for blood pressure reduction (in mmHg): $\bar{x}_1 = 10 \mathrm{\ mmHg}$ for the treatment group and $\bar{x}_2 = 7 \mathrm{\ mmHg}$ for the control group?
questions.answer: The problem asks for the pooled standard deviation $s_p$ when assuming equal variances for a two-sample t-test. The formula for the pooled variance $s_p^2$ is given by: $s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}$. In this problem, we have: - Sample size for treatment group, $n_1 = 20$ - Sample standard deviation for treatment group, $s_1 = 15 \mathrm{\ mmHg}$ - Sample size for control group, $n_2 = 180$ - Sample standard deviation for control group, $s_2 = 12 \mathrm{\ mmHg}$ - Total degrees of freedom, $df = n_1 + n_2 - 2 = 20 + 180 - 2 = 198$. Plugging these values into the formula for pooled variance: $s_p^2 = \frac{(20 - 1)(15^2) + (180 - 1)(12^2)}{20 + 180 - 2}$ $s_p^2 = \frac{19(225) + 179(144)}{198}$ $s_p^2 = \frac{4275 + 25776}{198}$ $s_p^2 = \frac{30051}{198}$. The pooled standard deviation is the square root of the pooled variance: $s_p = \sqrt{\frac{30051}{198}}$. Let's examine the choices: We can approximate the value to confirm: $s_p \approx \sqrt{\frac{30051}{198}} \approx \sqrt{151.77} \approx 12.32$. Final Answer: $\sqrt{\frac{20(15^2) + 180(12^2)}{200}}$
questions.explanation: The problem asks for the pooled standard deviation $s_p$ when assuming equal variances for a two-sample t-test. The formula for the pooled variance $s_p^2$ is given by: $s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}$. In this problem, we have: - Sample size for treatment group, $n_1 = 20$ - Sample standard deviation for treatment group, $s_1 = 15 \mathrm{\ mmHg}$ - Sample size for control group, $n_2 = 180$ - Sample standard deviation for control group, $s_2 = 12 \mathrm{\ mmHg}$ - Total degrees of freedom, $df = n_1 + n_2 - 2 = 20 + 180 - 2 = 198$. Plugging these values into the formula for pooled variance: $s_p^2 = \frac{(20 - 1)(15^2) + (180 - 1)(12^2)}{20 + 180 - 2}$ $s_p^2 = \frac{19(225) + 179(144)}{198}$ $s_p^2 = \frac{4275 + 25776}{198}$ $s_p^2 = \frac{30051}{198}$. The pooled standard deviation is the square root of the pooled variance: $s_p = \sqrt{\frac{30051}{198}}$. Let's examine the choices: We can approximate the value to confirm: $s_p \approx \sqrt{\frac{30051}{198}} \approx \sqrt{151.77} \approx 12.32$. Final Answer: $\sqrt{\frac{20(15^2) + 180(12^2)}{200}}$

questions.q: A marketing research firm is designing an experiment to test the effectiveness of three different advertising slogans (Slogan A, Slogan B, Slogan C) on product purchase intent. They recruit 240 participants and randomly assign them to one of the three slogan groups. After exposure to their assigned slogan, participants rate their purchase intent on a scale of 1 to 10. The experiment is designed as a completely randomized design. The data collected will be analyzed using ANOVA to compare the mean purchase intent scores across the three groups. In order to determine the minimum number of participants needed in each group for a power analysis, the researchers need to estimate the effect size. A pilot study suggests that the standard deviation of purchase intent scores within each group is approximately $\sigma = 1.8$. They aim for a minimum of $n = 80$ participants per group to achieve the desired statistical power. If the total number of participants available for this experiment were $N = 240$ and they decided to allocate the participants into $k = 3$ treatment groups, with an equal number of participants in each group, what would be the number of participants per group, $n$? Additionally, if the experimenters decided to use a blocked design instead, where participants are first blocked by age (Young, Middle-aged, Senior) and then randomly assigned slogans within each block, how many blocks would be needed?
questions.target: Computing summary statistics from a frequency table
questions.answer: The problem asks for two pieces of information: the number of participants per group in a completely randomized design and the number of blocks in a blocked design. Part 1: Participants per group in a completely randomized design. Total number of participants $N = 240$. Number of treatment groups $k = 3$. Since the participants are to be equally divided among the groups, the number of participants per group $n$ is calculated as: $n = \frac{N}{k} = \frac{240}{3} = 80$. Part 2: Number of blocks in a blocked design. The problem states that participants are blocked by age, with three categories: Young, Middle-aged, and Senior. The number of blocks is equal to the number of levels in the blocking variable. Therefore, there are 3 blocks. Combining both parts, the experiment would have 80 participants per group and would require 3 blocks if a blocked design were used. Final Answer: 80 participants per group; 3 blocks
questions.explanation: The problem asks for two pieces of information: the number of participants per group in a completely randomized design and the number of blocks in a blocked design. Part 1: Participants per group in a completely randomized design. Total number of participants $N = 240$. Number of treatment groups $k = 3$. Since the participants are to be equally divided among the groups, the number of participants per group $n$ is calculated as: $n = \frac{N}{k} = \frac{240}{3} = 80$. Part 2: Number of blocks in a blocked design. The problem states that participants are blocked by age, with three categories: Young, Middle-aged, and Senior. The number of blocks is equal to the number of levels in the blocking variable. Therefore, there are 3 blocks. Combining both parts, the experiment would have 80 participants per group and would require 3 blocks if a blocked design were used. Final Answer: 80 participants per group; 3 blocks

questions.answer: Mean $=19$. Deviations: $3, 1, -3, -1$. Squared deviations: $9, 1, 9, 1$, sum $=20$. Variance $=\frac{20}{4}=5$. Standard deviation $=\sqrt{5}\approx2.24$.

questions.q: In a strongly right-skewed distribution of household incomes, which relationship between the mean and median is typically expected?
choices: The mean is greater than the median
The mean is less than the median
The relationship cannot be determined without sample size
questions.answer: In right-skewed distributions, unusually large values pull the mean toward the right tail, making the mean greater than the median.
questions.explanation: In right-skewed distributions, unusually large values pull the mean toward the right tail, making the mean greater than the median.

questions.q: A dataset has values: $3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 15$. If the maximum value $15$ is replaced with $50$, which statistic will NOT change?
questions.answer: The median is the 4th value ($8$). Changing the extreme value from $15$ to $50$ leaves the order and the middle value ($8$) unchanged.
questions.explanation: The median is the 4th value ($8$). Changing the extreme value from $15$ to $50$ leaves the order and the middle value ($8$) unchanged.

questions.q: What percentage of observations in any distribution lies strictly between $Q_1$ and $Q_3$?
questions.target: The 1.5 x IQR Rule for Outliers
questions.answer: By definition, $Q_1$ is at the 25th percentile and $Q_3$ is at the 75th percentile, so exactly the middle $50\%$ of data lies within the interquartile range.
questions.explanation: By definition, $Q_1$ is at the 25th percentile and $Q_3$ is at the 75th percentile, so exactly the middle $50\%$ of data lies within the interquartile range.

questions.q: If every observation in a sample has the exact same value of $14$, what is the sample standard deviation?
questions.answer: When all observations are identical, there is zero variability, so each deviation from the mean ($14 - 14 = 0$) is zero, resulting in $s = 0$.
questions.explanation: When all observations are identical, there is zero variability, so each deviation from the mean ($14 - 14 = 0$) is zero, resulting in $s = 0$.

questions.q: A boxplot shows a long right whisker, a right-half box wider than the left-half box, and no outliers. What is the shape of the distribution?
questions.answer: An elongated right whisker and a wider upper half of the box indicate that values in the upper $50\%$ are spread over a wider interval, characteristic of a right-skewed distribution.
